units.text: Someone multiplied two matrices, A and B, and handed you the answer, C. Is C really A times B? You could multiply them again.

Nine entries, three multiplications each, twenty-seven in all. With a thousand rows and columns, a billion. Checking one entry at random is cheap, but it misses a single wrong entry eight times in nine.
Here is a better check. Toss a coin for each column of C, and add up the columns that land heads. Do the same to B, then multiply by A. That takes nine multiplications, not twenty-seven.
Both columns must match if C is right. They don't, so C is wrong, for certain. But that was one toss. Of the eight ways three coins can land, how many miss the wrong entry?
Check all eight. Four of them miss, exactly half. Because every miss leaves out the column that holds the wrong entry.
But no wrong answer hides from more than half the tosses. So toss again. Twenty fresh tosses all miss less than once in a million.
Look at the mistake on its own, C minus the true product. The check misses exactly when its heads columns add up to zero in every row.
Two in one row, both one too big, hide only when both coins land tails. Two of eight. But one too big and one too small hide whenever their coins agree. Four of eight, half again.
Now one, one and minus one in a row. How many tosses does it hide from?
Three. Not half, and not a power of two. Put one wrong entry in each row and column, and it hides only from all tails.
Why never more than half? Pick a column where C is wrong. Pair the tosses that differ only in its coin.
Because that row's sum changes across a pair by the wrong entry, both can't be zero. At most one of each pair misses.
Pairs cover every toss once, so at most half of all tosses miss, for matrices of any size.
